sentences.text: Soroavisaurus was estimated to be about 40 cm long, though size variation suggests some individuals were larger.
This extinct member of the avian clade Enantiornithes belongs to the family Avisauridae and is considered to occupy a basal position within that group.
The tarsometatarsus is a slender bone formed by the fusion of tarsal and metatarsal bones only in the upper portion of the fused element.
Metatarsal IV is flattened and slender, creating a distinct gap between it and metatarsal III in the upper part of the tarsometatarsus, a unique defining feature not found in other enantiornithines.
The trochlea of metatarsal IV has a triangular outline with a bony projection that nearly seals the gap between metatarsals III and IV.
The first toe consists of two phalanges forming a sharp, curved talon.
The species Soroavisaurus australis was named in 1993 by Luis M. Chiappe.
The only known species is known from fossils collected from the Lecho Formation in Estancia El Brete, southern Salta Province, Argentina.
The fossil deposits of the Lecho Formation at El Brete were discovered in 1975 by a team from the Fundación Miguel Lillo.
In 1981, Cyril Walker identified the bird fossils from El Brete as belonging to the group Enantiornithes.
The holotype of Soroavisaurus is the left tarsometatarsus specimen PVL-4690, measuring 46.9 mm in length.
Specimen PVL-4048 includes a 51.5 mm left tarsometatarsus associated with the hallux and four toe bones.
Specimen PVL-4048 was previously described as "Avisaurus sp." before being assigned to Soroavisaurus.
Soroavisaurus is hypothesized to have been a perching carnivore occupying an ecological niche similar to modern birds of prey.
Soroavisaurus is placed in the family Avisauridae as a close relative of the North American genus Avisaurus, though a 2024 study revised the family to include only six members.
Recent research suggests Intiornis is a more basal relative of the group leading to Avisauridae rather than the closest relative of Soroavisaurus.
Soroavisaurus lived in South America during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 71 to 69 million years ago, with deposits estimated to be between 71 and 69 million years old.
It lived in the Maastrichtian age on a warm, humid coastal plain featuring tropical forests, ponds, and lagoons near the Tropic of Capricorn.

It is debated whether Soroavisaurus is the same species as Enantiornis or Martinavis, though confirmation is difficult due to the lack of overlapping fossil parts, and a 2007 study suggested that Soroavisaurus might be a junior synonym of Enantiornis.
Researchers note that it is difficult to determine if wing fossils belong to Soroavisaurus, and some suggest a Martinavis species might represent its wings instead of Enantiornis.
The exact position of Soroavisaurus within the family Avisauridae is debated, with some authors placing it as an early-diverging member rather than close to North American forms like Avisaurus.
